# Methods (DRAFT; generated by tools/methods.py from the data files, do not edit by hand)

Run profile: full (5,000 Monte Carlo draws). Draft text of the methods and their results, in four parts generated from the data files (the deterministic numbers do not depend on the profile). Every figure: FIGURES.md; every output file: INDEX.md. References: docs/REFERENCES.md.

## Contents

* 1. Baseline projection
* 2. Planetary-boundary layer (AESA)
* 3. Pathways and the theoretical limit
* 4. Attribution principle, release accounting, replacement and the history (MODEL v3.2.0-v3.3.0)

## 1. Baseline projection

Every result below is read from the run outputs (outputs/data/; settings from projection.py). Adopted run: Reference (net replacement half-life 10 yr); 2026 overbuild rule `market_excess`.

### Summary

New Zealand is projected to build 81.5 million m² of new residential floor area in 2026–2050 in the Reference. In 2026–2050 this emits 19.8 Mt CO₂e: 19.4 Mt from materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss, counted in the construction year, and 359 kt of maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050. A further 7.5–8.2 Mt is committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4; outputs/reports/reconciliation.md). How fast existing dwellings are replaced is the largest structural uncertainty: Low replacement (the long-run rate throughout) gives 77.4 million m², High replacement (the 2018–2023 rate persisting) 86.7 million m², and Very High replacement (trend continues) (the weighted linear trend of the census-interval rates 1991–2023 continues) 92.2 million m². Within the Reference, joint uncertainty in the inputs gives a 90% interval of 60.3–104.7 million m² (median 81.3, mean 81.7). Outside the Monte Carlo, carbon-factor and soil bounds on the Reference carbon (19,761 kt): case-study jackknife 19,078–20,398 kt, single case study 15,602–23,616 kt, soil order 18,126–26,686 kt. Population uncertainty alone (Stats NZ 5th–95th percentiles) spans 55.2–108.5 million m². The joint interval is narrower than the population-only range because each population draw also moves household size along the matching Stats NZ Low/High variant: low-population variants come with smaller households (an older age structure), so the number of households varies less than population, whereas the population-only range holds household size on the Medium shape.

#### The 2026 overbuild rule

Building in the pipeline years 2026, 2027 is observed, not modelled: completions = 0.945 x consents lagged 17 months (consents observed to 2026–07–01): 2026 32,016 dwellings, +12,702 above the requirement; 2027 38,658 dwellings, +12,451 above the requirement. From 2028 building stays above the requirement by gap_ref x rho^(t-2027), with gap_ref = building 2027 - requirement 2028 = +11,848 and rho = 0.43 (the estimated persistence of departures from the calibrated identity). The 2026 overbuild is STOCK-ADDING: the extra dwellings join the stock as additional vacant dwellings, soil carbon loss applies (new footprints) and removals stay on the path of the replacement variant. The surplus is absorbed by 2035: the remaining surplus U(t) = C(t) (1 - w(t)), C the cumulative excess and w the normalised logistic (w = 0 up to the last observed year, w >= 2035 = 1), and the absorbed part is built less (payback, capped at the year's building, any shortfall carried). Market excess +34,229 and absorbed -34,229 dwellings over 2026–2050 (net -0), on top of whichever replacement variant runs. Stock-flow theory of the housing market (Rosen & Smith 1983; Wheaton 1990; DiPasquale & Wheaton 1992; Gabriel & Nothaft 2001) fixes the direction of the adjustment, the reversion of vacancy to its equilibrium rate, but not its speed: 2035 is the common RECC adoption window of the model and the speed is bracketed by sensitivity rows (never absorbed, by 2030, by 2045). Implied stock vacancy (1 - households / (stock + cumulative 2026 overbuild)) peaks at 6.63% in 2028 and is 5.39% in 2050, against 5.08–8.09% at the censuses 1986–2023 (pre-2013 values on the earlier empty definition).

The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); the 2026 overbuild raises implied stock vacancy temporarily and is absorbed by 2035, so implied vacancy returns to the parameter (5.39% in 2050). In 2050 implied stock vacancy is -0.0 percentage point above the 2023 rate; never absorbed (the MODEL v2.1 Reference) floor area would be +5.8%.

Caveats: the absorption speed is not identified by the eight census vacancy observations; over 2018–2023 part of the excess building went to redevelopment and household formation instead. rho is estimated on the calibrated identity, not on market cycles. Sensitivities: booking as stock-neutral redevelopment (implied net removals then peak at 16,194 in 2026), absorption never, by 2030 or by 2045, and the gap measured against the 2026 requirement.

#### Soil method

Soil carbon loss is the loss of soil organic carbon when land is built on (land-use change): a new building footprint seals the soil under it, while a rebuilt footprint sits on soil already sealed. Soil carbon loss is therefore applied to all floor area except the Demolition replacement band (demolition, net of unconsented additions) and the Recent replacement surge band, where it is zero. The factor is 58.77 kg CO₂e per m² of footprint, the area-weighted average over the 10 soil orders of the land zoned for urbanisation to about 2050 in Auckland, divided by each typology's floor space index (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026, Journal of Environmental Management 415, 130603, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130603). The Raw and Organic soil-order extremes are the bounding sensitivity. Carbon factors for materials come from 16 New Zealand case studies (Christoforatos & Pickering 2025, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment, https://doi.org/10.1108/SASBE-06-2025-0304).

### Validation

Rolling-origin hindcast of dwellings built (actual households and vacancy fed in; the net-replacement term predicted). Vacancy on a consistent definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share, 49.2% of unoccupied, at every census; the 2013 census share was 76.2%, and published empty vacancy falls 8.09% -> 5.08% across the 2013->2018 definitional break); vacancy as published in the last column.

| origin | test years | long-run rate (Low replacement rule) error | Reference rule error | best alternative | Reference rule, vacancy as published |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2006 | 2007–2023 | -3.9% | -4.2% | constant +1.0% | -14.9% |
| 2013 | 2014–2023 | +5.4% | +10.6% | constant +7.7% | -6.8% |
| 2018 | 2019–2023 | -10.5% | -11.4% | linked +2.9% | -11.3% |

Under a consistent vacancy definition the Reference rule reproduces building from the 2006 and 2013 origins to 2023 within 4–11%; the residual miss (-11.4% from 2018) is the 2018–23 surge.

Out-of-sample check (model run without 2026 data; completion lag 17 months): 2027 building observed in the pipeline 38,658 dwellings vs model 28,386; ratio 1.36.
Decomposition of the 2026 gap in the Reference (consents lagged 17 months): +6,545 dwellings = population -6,157 + pipeline from 2025 +12,702 + 2026 consents above requirement +0.

### Finding: 2026 building runs well above the model's requirement

With the 17-month completion lag, 2026 completions come from consents issued before 2026: observed 2026 building (consents lagged) is 32,016 dwellings against a Reference requirement of 25,470 (gap +6,545)[^low], all of it pipeline; 2027 pipeline building is 1.36 times what the Reference run without 2026 data implies. Population does not explain it: population growth over the year to June 2026 fell short of the projection, which lowers the requirement by 6,157. The gap is building already in the pipeline from 2025 (+12,702) plus 2026 consents above requirement (+0). Over 2018–2023 most building above household formation went to redevelopment (net removals 16,770) rather than vacancy (+6,286).

The model takes 2026 building from the observed consents and carries the excess forward as the 2026 overbuild (+12,702 dwellings in 2026, then gap_ref +11,848 fading at rho = 0.43; market excess +34,229 dwellings over 2026–2050, absorbed by 2035, net -0).

[^low]: In Low replacement (long-run rate) the requirement is 23,220 and the gap +8,795 = population -6,157 + pipeline +14,953 + 2026 consents above requirement +0.

### Planetary-boundary layer (AESA): climate change

Against the 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015), allocated to the sector by acquired rights (AR; Horup et al. 2025) and ability to pay (AtP; Hjalsted et al. 2021), the boundary is 172.4 kt CO₂e (AR) and 43.35 kt (AtP) in 2026, and 182.4 / 45.87 kt in 2050 (AtP = 25.1% of AR in every year). Over 2026–2050 the Reference exceeds them 4.46-fold (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 3.45–5.49) and 17.8-fold (AtP; 13.6–22.0). The two principles are a range and are not averaged. Methods, constants, sources and limitations: the AESA section of outputs/reports/METHODS_DRAFT.md; settings: outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md. The emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) by the 2026–2050 cohorts (7,502–8,220 kt) equal 41–45 years of the 2050 AR boundary; they fall after 2050 and are not part of the cumulative LoE 2026–2050.

### Open limitations and data needs

- No national demolition data: demolition of detached buildings up to three storeys is consent-exempt, so the implied replacement rates cannot be tested against a count.
- N4 (open): the Low/High household-size variants (deterministic) are paired with stochastic population percentiles through one draw z, and the total vs private-household population question is unresolved until the living-arrangement table (E2); the household projections are 2018-base, with Stats NZ's 2023-base release (late 2026) to be adopted in a later version.
- Timber end of life (C1–C4) excludes biogenic CO2 (confirmed by the author). Whether it includes landfill methane is TO CONFIRM from Christoforatos & Pickering 2025 (author check).
- With the typology mix held in every variant (internal to the model: it weights the case-study factors), neither the variants nor the Monte Carlo carry typology-mix uncertainty; a change of mix is a pathway question for later work, not a baseline uncertainty.
- The soil factor was derived for Auckland's future urban zones and is applied nationally.
- The case-study carbon factor for apartments rests on one independent case study (A_1 and A_2 are one design at two scales).
- The regional analysis of the recent replacement surge (replacement half-life by territorial authority) is deferred.
- Net replacement persistence (the replacement half-life of the Reference) is not identifiable from the census record; Low replacement and High replacement bound it.
- The 2018 census empty-dwelling count has no quality rating (DataInfo+); the vacancy terms rely on it.
- The 2026 overbuild fades at the persistence estimated on the calibrated stock identity (rho), not on market cycles (an assumption).
- Retirement-village floor area is reported but out of carbon scope.
- The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); the 2026 overbuild raises implied stock vacancy temporarily and is absorbed by 2035, so implied vacancy returns to the parameter (5.39% in 2050). The 2026 overbuild (market excess ≈34,200 dwellings over 2026–2050, of which ≈30,300 in 2026–2028) is absorbed by 2035 along the normalised logistic of the levers (≈34,200 dwellings built less; implied vacancy peaks at 6.63% in 2028). Stock-flow theory of the housing market (Rosen & Smith 1983; Wheaton 1990; DiPasquale & Wheaton 1992; Gabriel & Nothaft 2001) fixes the direction, reversion of vacancy to its equilibrium rate, not the speed; 2035 is the common RECC adoption window of the model and the speed is bracketed by sensitivity rows (never absorbed, by 2030, by 2045). The persistence rho = 0.43 describes how the flow deviation fades, not the payback of the stock.
- Decarbonisation paths are relative changes for European and global market processes modelled with premise on ecoinvent 3.9.1 (Horup et al. 2025); they are applied as relative changes to New Zealand case-study factors. This assumes NZ material supply decarbonises at the same relative rate as those markets, which is not tested.
- Items without a counterpart in Horup et al. follow a labelled proxy path (polymers, paint and SIP at EPS, the smallest reduction in the set; gypsum plasterboard at clay brick) or are held at 2025 (the lift); the proxies are a judgement, bracketed by holding them at 2025 (sensitivity).
- C1–C4 (end of life) is held at 2025 factors (no source for end-of-life decarbonisation); future end-of-life technology would lower the committed emissions (conservative).
- Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 gives the average of the 9 premise scenarios only; the scenario range is shown graphically in their Fig. 2, so no low/high decarbonisation path is implemented.
- Several items are made in New Zealand with electricity-intensive production (aluminium, Pink Batts glass wool, Pacific Steel rebar, WPMA Radiata timber, Nelson Pine LVL); the aluminium items are stated in their EPD names to use mainly renewables-generated electricity. Where their 2025 factors already reflect low-carbon electricity, the premise paths, which include the decarbonisation of electricity supply ("The Premise software accounts for future changes in several critical sectors (supply of conventional and alternative fuels, electricity, cement and steel production and freight and passenger road transportation), and includes implementation of technologies such as carbon capture and storage in steel and cement production" (Horup et al. 2025, p. 5)), may overstate their relative reduction; a sensitivity holds them at 2025.
- Composite floor decking (an RC item containing its steel deck and rebar) follows the concrete-structure path because the source gives no split; this is conservative versus steel profile for the steel share.
- Event timing is deterministic (n events evenly spaced in the building life). Resch et al. (2021, Section 2.2 and Fig. 4) model replacement years as probability-distributed; the L / n sensitivity brackets the timing within the service-life range implied by the counts, but not early or late failures.
- A4–A5 follows a generic technological-progress factor (Resch et al. 2021, Table 1) because it cannot be separated by material process; Horup et al. (2025, Fig. 2A, pp. 5–6) show that generic factors oversimplify material-specific trends, and Resch et al. state that "the decay functions should not be interpreted as predictions" (p. 4). Sensitivities: held at 2025 and the item S4 paths.
- Emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) are a range bounded by two conventions (2025 factors; the 2050 factors held), not a projection: the source paths end in 2050 and C1–C4 has no decarbonisation source.
- The repaint composition differs from the first coat but cannot be separated in the source file; repaints take the line's initial stage split (negligible: the paint path is the EPS proxy).
- Completion rate 0.945 and its band 0.93–0.96 rest on Auckland consents (Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025), applied nationally; the upper milestone is published only as ">95%" (0.96 is a stated edge).
- The 17-month consent-to-completion lag is the midpoint of the Auckland median of 1.27–1.53 yr (Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025), applied nationally as one fixed lag (no distribution of build times).

### Figures

The figures of the paper: outputs/paper/PAPER.md; Extended Data: outputs/extended_data/EXTENDED_DATA.md; every other figure: outputs/diagnostics/DIAGNOSTICS.md. Where the projection leaves the 1991–2025 range: outputs/reports/reality_checks.md.

## 2. Planetary-boundary layer (AESA)

The planetary-boundary layer is an absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA) of New Zealand new residential construction, climate change only, 2026–2050. Static carrying capacity; two allocation principles reported as a range and never averaged. This layer does not change the model; it reads the model's outputs.

### Equations as implemented (aesa.py)

**Acquired rights** (Horup et al. 2025, Sci. Total Environ. 966, 178780, Eq. 1, p. 4):

    B_AR(t) = SOS · (Ī_sec,base / I_glob) · [P_NZ(t) / P_NZ(t0)] · [P_W(t0) / P_W(t)],   t0 = 2025

Ī_sec,base is the mean annual sector impact 2016–2025 from this model's own history (same scope, accounting rule and soil convention as the projection; at 2025 case-study factors: past construction used past technology, so the decarbonisation of A1–A3 applies only to 2026–2050). Over the base window LoE_AR = I_glob / SOS = 8.1938 by construction (the sector impact cancels); the information is in the trajectory relative to the base.

**Ability to pay** (Hjalsted et al. 2021, J. Ind. Ecol. 25, 6–19, Table 2 Eqs. 5–6, p. 11; SI Eq. S1):

    SoSOS_ind(t) = SOS / P_W(t) · (g_W / g_NZ) · α
    B_AtP(t)     = SoSOS_ind(t) · P_NZ(t) · s_sec
    α            = 1 / Σ_c [(P_c / P_W) (g_W / g_c)]   (SI Eq. S1 with GDP totals, rewritten per capita)

g = GDP per capita in base year b = 2024, held fixed; g_W = Σ P_c g_c / Σ P_c and P_W = Σ P_c over the same covered economies. B_AtP / B_AR = (g_W/g_NZ) · α · s_sec · (P_NZ(t0)/P_W(t0)) · (I_glob/Ī_sec,base) is constant in this static design: 0.2514.

**Carbon factors.** A1–A3 of each case-study EPD item decarbonised 2026–2050 after Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 (item-level mapping, data/material_item_map.csv: direct, Horup p. 6, proxy or held), for construction and for the A1–A3 share of maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events); A4–A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) after Resch et al. (2021) Table 1; C1–C4, held items and soil carbon loss at 2025 (see outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md).

**Accounting.** Time-resolved: the sector impact I_sec(t) counts the materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss of the construction in year t and the maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events) that occurs in year t in buildings built from 2026. Maintenance events after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, reported below as a range and in years of the 2050 AR boundary; they are not part of the cumulative LoE.

**Level of exceedance**: LoE_k(t) = I_sec(t) / B_k(t); cumulative LoE = Σ I_sec / Σ B_k over 2026–2050 (ratio of sums).

**Dating.** Model year t is 31 December (Stats NZ ERP history). The WPP 2024 series (1 July) and, in the sensitivities, the Stats NZ (30 June) and WPP New Zealand series are dated at t as the mean of mid-year t and t+1.

### Results

The 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015) allocated by acquired rights gives 172.4 kt CO₂e in 2026 and 182.4 kt in 2050; by ability to pay 43.35 and 45.87 kt (25.1% of AR in every year). Both rise: New Zealand's share of world population grows between 2026 and 2050. Over 2026–2050 the Reference emits 19,761 kt against cumulative boundaries of 4,427 kt (AR) and 1,113 kt (AtP): cumulative LoE 4.46 (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 3.45–5.49) and 17.8 (AtP; 13.6–22.0).

| variant | cumulative LoE AR | cumulative LoE AtP |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | 4.46 | 17.8 |
| Low replacement | 4.27 | 17.0 |
| High replacement | 4.69 | 18.7 |
| Very High replacement (trend continues) | 4.93 | 19.6 |
| Reference, replacement half-life 5 yr | 4.38 | 17.4 |
| Reference, replacement half-life 15 yr | 4.52 | 18.0 |
| Low replacement, no census under-construction correction | 4.27 | 17.0 |
| Reference, no census under-construction correction | 4.46 | 17.8 |
| High replacement, no census under-construction correction | 4.69 | 18.7 |

#### Committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4; deterministic)

Lower bound: maintenance events (B2, B4) after 2050 with the 2050 factors held; upper bound: at 2025 factors; C1–C4 at 2025 factors in both. Years of the 2050 AR boundary = committed / B_AR(2050). Not part of the cumulative LoE.

### Limitations

- Static carrying capacity: the carrying capacities are constant yearly values modelled at steady state and their timespan may not match the assessment period (Clausen et al. 2025, pp. 143 and 148).
- Accounting (time-resolved): the sector impact of 2026–2050 counts materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss in the construction year and maintenance (B2, B4) in the year it occurs. Maintenance after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, outside 2026–2050; they are reported as a range (outputs/data/aesa/results.json "committed", Fig3c) in years of the 2050 AR boundary and are not compared with the 2026–2050 boundary. Whole life at construction is a sensitivity.
- History at 2025 factors: the acquired-rights base (2016–2025) and the base-window sensitivities use the 2025 case-study factors because no historical factor series exists for the case studies. If past production was more carbon-intensive than in 2025 (as the ~1%/yr technological progress assumed by Resch et al. 2021 implies), the base and hence the AR boundary are understated and the AR exceedance overstated (conservative); the size of this effect is not quantified. The base follows the projection's accounting rule (materials and construction and soil carbon loss of the base window's construction plus the maintenance within the base window of the cohorts built in it).
- The primary SOS (6.81E12) is the 2 °C carrying capacity of Bjørn & Hauschild (2015), not the 1 W/m² planetary boundary (3.61E12, sensitivity C). Sala et al. (2020, Table 3) label 6.81E12 as radiative forcing after Rockström et al. (2009), which does not match its derivation in Bjørn & Hauschild (2015).
- GWP basis: Bjørn & Hauschild (2015) ESM2 uses AR5 GWP100 factors (CH4 28, N2O 265; column "CFs (GWP100, IPCC5)") while their Table 1 cites Forster et al. (2007), i.e. AR4. The GWP basis of the case-study LCA factors used by the model is not documented in this repository (building_data.xlsx gives "GWP" columns only; source Christoforatos & Pickering 2025): to be confirmed by the author.
- I_glob = 5.58E13 (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015 ESM2, from Laurent et al. 2013, year 2010): Laurent et al. (2013) is not in hand, so whether it includes land-use-change CO2 (the sector impact includes soil carbon loss) and its GWP basis are NOT VERIFIED. The per-gas indicator scores in ESM2 sum to 54.0 Gt CO2-eq with 39.5 Gt CO2; a CO2 total of that size is consistent with inclusion of land-use-change CO2 (inference, not a sourced statement). The EC-JRC table "Normalization factors for testing" (Benini, Sala & Pant, version 0.1.1, 15 Dec 2015; sheet 1.3) gives the PROSUITE global value as 5.589E13 kg CO2-eq, 8,100 kg/person, "2010 or 2000".
- Final-consumption-expenditure upscaling: the numerator (consented residential value) is an investment flow (gross fixed capital formation), while Hjalsted et al. (2021) define the upscaling on final consumption and leave intermediate sectors as open (p. 16).
- Ability to pay: Hjalsted et al. (2021) state GDP as "USD/cap (2017)", World Bank (2019), without naming the series; current US$ is the sensitivity. The GDP coverage excludes economies without the measure (listed in outputs/data/aesa/results.json).
- Monte Carlo: I_sec,base is recomputed in every draw with that draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology), so the factor uncertainty is treated alike in the base and the projection; it does not co-vary with the draw's completion rate or dwelling size (historical floor area is observed).
- The numerical results in Hjalsted et al.'s SI (Tables S4-S9) are reproduced only with α = 1; we apply α as specified in their Eq. 5 and SI Eq. S1, which ensures national shares sum to the global SOS. The authors have been contacted.

### Notes

- The manuscript world population 2025 (8,231,613,070) equals the WPP 2024 Median sheet x 1000; its 2026–2028 values differ from it by +/-0.5 person, consistent with a source at a higher precision than the 3-decimal thousands in this file; they are not a dating convention (the mean of 1 July t and t+1 differs by ~34 M).
- In the Monte Carlo the AR boundary varies with each draw's NZ population path and with I_sec,base recomputed from the draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology) on the observed history; the AtP boundary varies with population only. mc_base_fixed gives the bands with I_sec,base held at its deterministic value.

## 3. Pathways and the theoretical limit

### The lever rule

Ambition levels follow the 2050 Pathways Calculator (DECC 2010; DESNZ 2023) and EUCalc (D2.5, 2020): Reference = Level 1, Moderate = Level 2, Ambitious = Level 3, theoretical limit (TL) = Level 4. Ambitious is the best value already achieved, by the first applicable sub-rule: A, a case-study distribution exists: the Harrell-Davis q0.15 quantile of the pooled scale-free case ratios (the top-15% convention of the EU Taxonomy, Delegated Regulation 2021/2139, Annex I s. 7.7), with a percentile bootstrap interval; B, an NZ record with no structural trend exists: the best value ever observed in NZ; C, otherwise: a published reference value (official projection > legislated target > peer-reviewed scenario > peer-country value). Moderate is the exact midpoint between the Reference and Ambitious in the lever's native parameter (per year for the path levers L1 and L9). TL is the definitional zero or full where one exists, else the best single observation, and is asserted at least as strong as Ambitious. Every level moves from the Reference along the normalised logistic 2026 -> 2035 (midpoint 2030.5, k = ln(81)/6).

Levels between the Reference and Ambitious are indexed by lambda in [0, 1]: x(lambda) = x_ref + lambda (x_amb - x_ref), so Moderate is lambda = 0.5 exactly (tested for every lever); the lambda-sweep of each lever is in the Extended Data.

### The levers and the PAS 2080 strategies

The nine levers are grouped by the carbon reduction hierarchy of PAS 2080:2023 (BSI 2023, Clause 4.3 and Figure 5: Avoid - Switch - Improve). Classification rule: Avoid = levers that reduce the floor area needed to house the population, system level (number of dwellings) before asset level (floor area per dwelling); Switch = alternative site and materials for the floor area that is built (carbon per m²); Improve = construction efficiencies. Within a strategy the order follows the decision sequence (system before asset; site before materials). Avoid acts on floor area, Switch and Improve on carbon per m², the two axes of Fig6. The lever settings (Moderate, Ambitious and TL values, sub-rules and anchors) are those of MODEL v3.0.0; only the grouping, numbering, names and order changed (MODEL v3.3.0; docs/RENAMING.md).

#### S1 Avoid

**L1 Household size (sub-rule C).** S_Ambitious(t) = S_Ref(t) + [S_High(t) - S_Medium(t)], the gap between the Stats NZ High and Medium household-size variants (same living-arrangement assumption; projection runs rebased on the 2023 census), held at its 2043 value after 2043; High >= Medium in every year (asserted). 2050: Reference 2.6518, Moderate 2.6725, Ambitious 2.6933; TL1 S = 2.7905 (the 1991 maximum of the model history).

**L2 Vacancy rate (sub-rule B).** Ambitious 4.01%, the 1996 census minimum on one definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share of unoccupied private dwellings applied to every census); Moderate (v_ref + v_min)/2 = 4.70%; TL2 v = 0. Reference = the published 2023 census value 5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is 5.38%.

**L3 Building lifetime (sub-rule C).** Demolition and the recent-surge component of net replacement x (1 - d), d = 0.40 (Pellan et al. 2024: 150,000 -> 90,000 demolitions a year), Moderate 0.20; TL3: zero demolition, no redevelopment wave; unconsented additions kept at the long-run rate. The census net replacement rates are context only.

**L4 Extra space (sub-rule B).** The Ambitious size is the smallest annual mean new-dwelling size ever consented, by typology, 1990–2025 (consented floor area / consents): Detached 148.8 m² (1990), Townhouses 105.8 m² (1990), Apartments 91.0 m² (1998). The Reference size is the 2023–2025 mean (Detached 187.6 m²), (Townhouses 108.0 m²), (Apartments 95.8 m²). The lever removes a share f of the extra-space margin (size - occupied area, occupied area = household size x OLF), f_t = (size_ref - size_min) / (size_ref - occ_ref), occ_ref = S_ref(2035) x OLF_t, so that the size at full strength equals the minimum; f_Ambitious = Detached 0.4268, Townhouses 0.1091, Apartments 0.1153; Moderate f/2; TL f = 1 (size = occupied area). It acts on the margin after L5. 1990 is the first year of the consent series and a recession year.

**L5 Occupancy density (sub-rule A).** For each of the 16 case studies (10 detached, 4 townhouses, 2 apartments; A_2 included as a distinct design) the design floor area per occupant (OLF) is divided by the median of its typology; r_Ambitious = HD q0.15 = 0.8194 (95% bootstrap interval 0.732–0.960, B = 2000); r_Moderate = (1 + r)/2 = 0.9097. The ratio scales every typology's OLF and dwelling size; TL5 per typology = min(own densest design ratio, r_Ambitious): Detached 0.7095, Townhouses 0.8194, Apartments 0.8194.

#### S2 Switch

**L6 Brownfield-first development (sub-rule C).** Share of new floor area on previously developed land: Ambitious 0.59 (England 2018–21, DLUHC 2022); Moderate (s_ref + 0.59)/2 = 0.350 with s_ref = 0.110 (the v3 Reference: replacement (soil-free) floor area / total, ratio of sums 2026–2050); TL6 s = 1. Context: US EPA (2014) infill share 21%. lambda = 0 is the lever off (the Reference); a constant s = s_ref would act in the years whose own replacement share is below s_ref. TL6 = 100% brownfield makes TL7 zero within TL.

**L7 Soil-aware planning (sub-rule C).** Soil carbon loss per m² x (1 - x), x = 0.146 (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026), Moderate 0.073; TL7 the lowest soil order (Detached 22.9, Townhouses 13.8, Apartments 2.5 kg CO₂e/m²).

**L8 Material carbon efficiency (sub-rule A).** r = HD q0.15 of the 14 independent detached and townhouse case ratios A1-A3_i / pooled A1–A3 of the typology = 0.8270 (95% 0.607–0.950); Moderate (1 + r)/2 = 0.9135; TL8 Detached 0.530, Townhouses 0.827, Apartments 0.827 (detached: the best case, SD_2).

#### S3 Improve

**L9 Construction-stage carbon (sub-rule C).** Ambitious: A4–A5 linear to zero by 2050 (Zero Carbon Act s. 5Q; City of Oslo 2025); Moderate: the per-year midpoint of the Reference path e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) and Ambitious (2050 factor 0.389); TL9 A4–A5 = 0. A5 treated as energy: site waste assumed eliminated (upper bound).

### One run: payback and re-occupation

Every run follows the same order per year: gross_t -> overbuild payback -> re-occupation -> built_t. The 2026 overbuild of the Reference (the market excess) is computed once and held fixed in every run (the largest difference between runs is 0.0 dwellings); its absorption follows the Reference weights, the payback capped at max(gross_t, 0) with any shortfall carried. In the TL-family runs the dwellings released by TL1 (household decline) and TL2 (zero vacancy) to 2050, R = R1 + R2 (the overbuild is not in R), meet a constant share of each year's need after the payback, s = min(R, G+)/G+, G+ = sum over 2027–2050 of max(gross_t, 0); the cumulative re-occupied never exceeds the cumulative released: where that binds the shortfall is built and s is recomputed from the remaining pool; R > G+ leaves a surplus vacant in 2050. Re-occupied dwellings are attributed to TL1 and TL2 in proportion R1 : R2.

TL: R1 = 0, R2 = 116,869, G+ = 337,178, s = 0.482; the release constraint binds in no year; need is non-positive (nothing built) in no year; surplus vacant 2050 0. Instant TL (sensitivity): R1 = 62,085, R2 = 114,399, s = 0.604.

## 4. Attribution principle, release accounting, replacement and the history (MODEL v3.2.0-v3.3.0)

#### Attribution principle and system boundary (unchanged from MODEL v3.0.0)

Emissions fully determined at construction (A1–A5, soil carbon loss) are attributed to the construction year; emissions depending on later decisions or technology (B, C1–C4) are time-resolved (in-window counted, remainder committed). System boundary: new residential construction, identical for the AR/AtP base (2016–2025) and the projection (2026–2050). Demand uses the existing stock (vacancy, overbuild absorption, re-occupation, replacement); emissions of the existing stock are outside scope on both sides. The committed emissions of an investment decision are attributed to the decision (Davis & Socolow 2014, Environ. Res. Lett. 9, 084018 [verify]).

#### Release accounting (bands.py; pathways.run)

Positive demand bands are always gross need: population growth, smaller households, extra space, vacancy (the gross allowance: on new households and any vacancy-rate rise), the 2026 overbuild, demolition replacement and the recent replacement surge. Every release is its own negative band, booked in the year it is used: 'Overbuild absorbed' (the payback, taken on the gross need), 'Unconsented additions' (the calibrated residual of the census identity), 'Vacancy released' (a vacancy-rate fall in a run without any lever at its theoretical limit: used in the year it occurs, capped at that year's gross need, the rest carried forward) and 'Released dwellings (TL)' (the re-occupation pool). No release is netted inside a positive band and no band is rescaled: retirement-village units are a constant share of every dwelling built, so each in-scope band is its gross floor area times (1 - that share), exactly. If gross need minus usable releases is negative in a year, nothing is built and the unusable amount is carried forward against the next years: released dwellings remain available later, as they do in the theoretical-limit re-occupation pool. Whatever is still unusable in 2050 is booked in 2050 against its release band and as 'Surplus kept vacant (2050)', so the bands add up to the total in every year (checked to 1e-9). In every theoretical-limit-family run (TL, the TL steps of both waterfalls, every TL Shapley subset) the re-occupation pool holds every dwelling release present in the run (a vacancy-rate fall at any level, a household-size fall), with the constant-share rule, the availability constraint and attribution in proportion to the release of each source. The Reference, every lever and pathway run and TL are unchanged from MODEL v3.0.0 (tested to 1e-9); the TL waterfall steps and the TL1-TL9 Shapley values from the Moderate Pathway change (MODEL v3.2.0), and in the pathway Monte Carlo the draws with a negative-gross year (docs/CHANGELOG_v3_2.md).

#### Zero-year guard (engine.forward)

A year whose built floor area is below 1e-06 m² is a year in which nothing is built: its floor area, soil-bearing share and soil carbon are set to 0. The soil-bearing share is clipped to [0, 1] in every run. Without the guard the share 1 - soil-free / total is a ratio of floating-point noise and the soil carbon of a year without construction is non-zero (a MODEL v3.0.0 defect, found in pathway Monte Carlo draws; no deterministic run is affected).

#### History by census interval (validation.history_bands)

The residual band of the history is split into the census-measured net replacement (the interval rate of the census dwelling-count identity x the previous year's stock x the year's dwelling size; it may be negative, e.g. 1996–2001), the retirement-village units (negative, out of scope) and the unexplained building (the remainder to the observed in-scope floor area built; it may be negative, e.g. 2013–2018). The bands add up to the observed floor area built in every interval (checked to 1e-9). Over 1992–2025 the unexplained building sums to -3,709 dwellings (-0.46% of the 803,534 built); the floor-area remainder equals the unexplained dwellings of the stock identity x the dwelling size (difference 3.5e-15 Mm²).

#### Replacement in the Reference and its variants (MODEL v3.3.0)

Net replacement fades from the 2018–23 census rate (0.17%) to the long-run 1991–2023 rate (0.06%), half-life 10 yr; BRANZ demolition (0.135%) only splits the net rate into the demolition, surge and unconsented-additions bands. The half-life is not identifiable from the census record (seven censuses, six interval rates), so the Monte Carlo samples it, U(5, 15) yr, with the deterministic 10 yr as its median (it acts in the Reference variant only). The functional form matters little for the cumulative surge: the mean excess over the long-run rate 2026–2050 is 0.052 pp with the 10-yr half-life and 0.055 pp for a linear path that reaches the long-run rate in 2050.

Very High replacement (trend continues; a sensitivity variant): the 6 census-interval rates 1991–2023 fitted by weighted least squares on the mean of each interval's years (weights = interval length), rate = -0.121385 + 6.0725e-05 x year, extrapolated 2026–2050: 0.164% in 2026 and 0.310% in 2050. It is not adopted as the Reference: 6 interval rates (7 censuses), 2 of them negative (1996–2001, 2001–2006), the 2013–2018 census definition break (empty / residents-away dwellings), and the unbounded extrapolation of a policy-driven wave.

#### Completion rate in the Monte Carlo

Uniform on [0.93, 0.96] (MODEL v4.0.0). The bounds are published completion milestones for Auckland consents (Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025, Policy Quarterly 21(1), 63–68, footnote 12): 93% of 2018–2019 consents had a final inspection by July 2024 (lower bound of eventual completion) and more than 95% of 2018–2021 consents had a first inspection (upper bound; the article gives no point value, so the edge 0.96 is a stated judgement). The deterministic central value 0.945 is their midpoint, and so the median of the Monte Carlo input. No shape inside the band is identified, hence uniform. Limitation: Auckland evidence applied nationally.

#### Consent-to-completion lag and pipeline years (MODEL v4.0.0)

Completions in month m = 0.945 x consents in month m - L, L = 17 months, aggregated to calendar years. L is the midpoint of the median time to dwelling completion of 1.27–1.53 yr for Auckland consents as of July 2024 (Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025, citing Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023), consistent with the Stats NZ Experimental building indicators (dwelling-weighted median 455 days from consent to final inspection for December 2020 quarter consents, 533 days for September 2022 quarter consents). The same lag applies everywhere consents become dwellings: the stock identity, the census-interval net replacement rates (consents lagged L/12 years before each census date), the dwelling-size and typology-mix windows, historical floor area and the AR / AtP base, and the projection start. Projection years whose twelve lagged months are all observed (2026, 2027) are pipeline years: their building is observed in every run (the market excess over the requirement), and the excess fades from the next year at the persistence rho re-estimated on the lagged history. Before April 1990 the typology columns of the consent file are empty; those months are split by the April 1990 - March 1991 typology ratios of all dwellings (they enter only the 1991 completions, which are used in the cumulative floor area from 1991 and nowhere else). Limitations: one fixed lag (no distribution of build times), Auckland evidence applied nationally. The rolling-origin hindcast of the census dwelling-count identity is not worse at L = 17 than at L = 0 (outputs/data/baseline/completion_lag_hindcast.csv).

#### Theoretical limit: constraints at Level 4 (MODEL v4.0.0)

Level 4 is the definitional limit of each lever, reached along the common adoption window, except household size (TL1): its level (2.7905, the 1991 census maximum) is approached no faster than the fastest change of household size observed between consecutive censuses 1991–2023 (0.01176 per year, 1996–2001; census-benchmarked households): S_TL(t) = min(S_ref(2026) + r (t - 2026), level), never below the Ambitious path. The level is reached in 2035.6. Household size is a population-level outcome of age structure, partnering and housing costs; the speed limit keeps the theoretical limit within changes the New Zealand census record has shown. The instant-TL row keeps its definition (every level from 2027). In every theoretical-limit-family run the Reference's overbuild surplus (the positive market excess of the pipeline years and of the fading gap) enters the re-occupation pool with the TL1 / TL2 releases (constant share of each year's positive need, availability constraint, carry-forward); the re-occupied overbuild is booked in 'Overbuild absorbed'. Releases of an observed (pipeline) year enter the pool in the first unobserved year.

#### Household-size projection (MODEL v4.0.0 note)

Household size follows the Stats NZ 2018-base household projection shape (Medium variant), rebased on the 2023 census; it is to be replaced by the 2023-base household projections when published. Sensitivities: the Stats NZ Low / High variants and the 2018–2023 census pace continued linearly from 2023, for the Reference, the Moderate / Ambitious Pathway and TL (sensitivity/household_size.csv).

#### Check and sensitivity rows

TL with re-occupation as fast as demand allows (deterministic sensitivity row): 3,766.9 kt, LoE AR 0.851 (TL: 4,422.9 kt, LoE AR 0.999).

L8 with the apartment case A_1 (n = 15): r = 0.841 against the adopted 0.827 (n = 14); report only (A_1's ratio to its pooled value is 1.0000 by construction).
